text: Quantum computers get their own complexity class, and understanding exactly what it does and doesn't contain is the difference between a realistic view of quantum computing and science-fiction hype.

BQP stands for bounded-error quantum polynomial time. A problem is in BQP if a quantum computer, using a number of gates that's polynomial in the input size, outputs the correct answer with probability at least two-thirds. Bounded-error doesn't mean weak: because of error amplification, running the same algorithm several independent times and taking the majority vote shrinks the chance of a wrong answer exponentially, the same way it does for classical randomized algorithms. That's why the exact constant, two-thirds or any other fixed value above one-half, doesn't matter for the definition.

Several relationships here are proven, not conjectured. P is contained in BPP, which is contained in BQP, so quantum computers can do anything classical deterministic or randomized computers can do in polynomial time. BQP is contained in PSPACE, meaning any BQP computation can be simulated with only polynomial memory classically, even if it takes exponential time. And BQP sits inside PP, a looser classical class, a containment proven by Adleman, DeMarrais, and Huang in 1997.

Here's where it gets genuinely open: whether BQP contains NP is unknown. Factoring, the problem Shor's algorithm solves, is in BQP and also in NP intersect co-NP — but that overlap doesn't prove BQP contains NP-complete problems, because factoring was specifically chosen as an example that sits in that overlap. The best general-purpose quantum tool for brute-force search over NP-complete problems is Grover's algorithm, and its quadratic speedup — root N queries instead of N — still leaves an exponential search. BQP is not believed to contain NP-complete problems at all.
Next lesson sorts quantum speedup into its real categories — exponential, quadratic, and none — so you can tell a genuine claim from marketing.
